mcqs.q: The most commonly used scalpel handle in oral surgery is the:
mcqs.explain: The Bard–Parker No. 3 handle receives blades Nos. 11, 12 and 15.

mcqs.q: Which scalpel blade is most commonly used for flaps and incisions around teeth?
mcqs.explain: No. 15 is the workhorse blade for flaps and incisions around teeth and on edentulous ridges.

mcqs.q: A small stab incision to drain an abscess is best made with blade:
mcqs.explain: The sharp-pointed No. 11 blade is used for stab incisions such as incising an abscess.

mcqs.q: The hooked No. 12 blade is particularly indicated for:
opts: Incisions in the gingival sulcus and posterior to teeth (tuberosity)
mcqs.explain: The hooked No. 12 blade suits the gingival sulcus and areas posterior to the teeth (e.g. maxillary tuberosity).

mcqs.q: The most commonly used periosteal elevator is the:
mcqs.explain: The No. 9 Molt periosteal elevator (pointed and broad ends) is the standard for reflecting a mucoperiosteal flap.

mcqs.q: Which retractor looks like a periosteal elevator but must NOT be used to elevate the mucoperiosteum?
opts: Seldin retractor (its edge is not sharp)
mcqs.explain: The Seldin retractor resembles an elevator but has a blunt edge — it is a retractor, not an elevator.

mcqs.q: The delicate forceps used to gently stabilize soft tissue for suturing are the:
mcqs.explain: Adson forceps (with or without fine teeth) gently hold tissue; toothed ones grip more delicately than untoothed.

mcqs.q: Allis tissue forceps should NEVER be used on tissue that will remain in the mouth because they:
mcqs.explain: Locking, toothed Allis forceps crush tissue; use them for excised tissue/biopsy or the tongue, not tissue that stays.

mcqs.q: The hemostat most commonly used to control bleeding from a small vessel is the:
mcqs.explain: The curved 'mosquito' hemostat is the common artery forceps; most dentoalveolar bleeding is first controlled by pressure.

mcqs.q: Why should the air-turbine (restorative) handpiece NOT be used to remove bone?
opts: Exhausted air may be forced into tissue planes, causing air emphysema
It cannot cut bone at all
It is impossible to sterilize burs
mcqs.explain: Air driven into the wound can cause dangerous surgical (air) emphysema; use a sterilizable surgical handpiece that does not exhaust air into the field.

mcqs.q: When cutting bone with a bur, a saline coolant is used to:
mcqs.explain: Burs generate heat; saline irrigation prevents thermal bone necrosis.

mcqs.q: The bi-bevel chisel (osteotome) is specifically used for:
opts: Smoothing bone on a pull stroke
mcqs.explain: The bi-bevel chisel/osteotome sections multi-rooted teeth; mono-bevel chisels remove bone.

mcqs.q: A bone file removes bone effectively only on the:
mcqs.explain: Bone-file teeth cut on the pull stroke; pushing only burnishes/crushes bone.

mcqs.q: The main use of a periapical curette is to remove:
opts: Granulation tissue, small cysts, bone chips and foreign bodies from bony cavities
mcqs.explain: The spoon-shaped curette debrides sockets/bone defects of granulation tissue, small cysts, bone chips and foreign bodies.

mcqs.q: Compared with a hemostat, the beaks of a needle holder are:
opts: Short with a grooved/crosshatched inner surface for a firm needle grip
Longer and thinner with parallel grooves
Sharp and pointed like a blade
mcqs.explain: Needle-holder beaks are short and crosshatched to grip the needle; hemostat beaks are thin, long and parallel-grooved.

mcqs.q: Which is an ABSORBABLE suture material?
mcqs.explain: Absorbable: Monocryl, Vicryl, Chromic, PDS (break down by hydrolysis). Silk, nylon, Prolene, steel are non-absorbable.

mcqs.q: The most commonly used non-resorbable suture in the oral cavity, and the usual mucosal size, are:
mcqs.explain: Black silk is the common intraoral non-resorbable suture; 3-0 (000) is the usual size for oral mucosa.

mcqs.q: A disadvantage of polyfilament (braided) suture is that it:
opts: Exhibits capillary action that can wick fluid and spread bacteria
mcqs.explain: Braided sutures handle and knot well but their capillary action can draw fluid/bacteria along the strand; monofilament has low friction but poor knot holding.

mcqs.q: The triangular (Cryer) elevator is most useful when:
opts: A broken root remains and the adjacent socket is empty
Both sockets are full of intact teeth
Removing cortical bone over a torus
mcqs.explain: Its tip is placed in the empty adjacent socket and rotated to engage the cementum of the retained root.

mcqs.q: The buccal beak of a maxillary molar forceps is pointed in order to:
opts: Fit into the buccal bifurcation of the two buccal roots
mcqs.explain: The pointed buccal beak engages the buccal furcation; the concave palatal beak fits the palatal root. Maxillary molar forceps are left- and right-specific.

mcqs.q: Which forceps are the longest, with smooth concave bayonet beaks usable on both sides?
mcqs.explain: The maxillary third-molar bayonet forceps are longest (posterior position) with smooth concave beaks, so they serve both left and right.

mcqs.q: A scalpel should be held with which grasp, and why?
opts: A pen grasp, for maximal control
A palm grasp, for maximal force
A reverse grasp, to protect the tissues
mcqs.explain: Mobile tissue should be held firmly and the blade pressed down firmly.

mcqs.q: Which scalpel blade is used for EXTRAORAL skin incisions?
mcqs.explain: No. 15 is the most commonly used intraorally, No. 12 is hooked for sulcular incisions, and No. 11 is sharp-pointed for stab incisions.

mcqs.q: On the No. 9 Molt periosteal elevator, the POINTED end is used to:
opts: Start the reflection and reflect the dental papillae between teeth in a prying motion
Continue elevating the periosteum from bone
mcqs.explain: The broad rounded end continues the elevation, with its convex surface toward the flap.

mcqs.q: Which retractor is a broad, heart-shaped, serrated instrument that engages and retracts the tongue?
mcqs.explain: Austin is a right-angle retractor and Minnesota an offset retractor, both for cheek and flap.

mcqs.q: The Stillies pickup differs from the Adson forceps in that it is:
opts: Longer, for handling tissue in the more posterior mouth
Angled for picking objects off the tray
mcqs.explain: The college pliers are the angled forceps for picking up small objects, and are not especially useful for handling tissue.

mcqs.q: The most commonly used instrument for removing bone in dentoalveolar surgery is the:
mcqs.explain: It has sharp blades squeezed together by the handles, cutting or pinching through bone.

mcqs.q: Which burs are used for bone removal in oral surgery?
opts: No. 557 or No. 703 fissure bur and a No. 8 round bur
mcqs.explain: For large amounts, such as torus palatinus reduction, a large bone bur resembling an acrylic bur is used, and saline coolant is necessary to avoid bone necrosis.

mcqs.q: The three parts of a dental elevator are the:
mcqs.explain: Handle, hinge and beaks are the components of extraction forceps.

mcqs.q: The most commonly used elevator for removing teeth and roots in both jaws is the:
mcqs.explain: Its blade has two surfaces, one convex and one concave, and it is held with the index finger along the blade.

mcqs.q: The T-bar (cross-bar) elevator generates more force and is:
opts: Used only for maxillary third molars
Used only to reflect the periosteum
mcqs.explain: It is introduced through the empty socket of one root of a multi-rooted mandibular molar to engage and remove the interseptal bone and the other root.

mcqs.q: Pick-type (Apexo) elevators are mainly used to:
opts: Remove root tips in both jaws
mcqs.explain: They are also called double-angled elevators; the shank has a double angle with narrow blades.

mcqs.q: The basic components of extraction forceps are the:
mcqs.explain: Because tooth anatomy varies, forceps have specially designed beaks for specific teeth.

mcqs.q: Mandibular molar forceps are distinguished by:
opts: Right-angled beaks, BOTH with sharp points for the buccal and lingual bifurcation
One pointed buccal beak and one concave palatal beak
Straight handles with concave rounded beaks
A long, slightly curved bayonet shape
mcqs.explain: The maxillary molar forceps have one pointed buccal beak and a concave palatal beak and come as a left and right pair.

mcqs.q: For oral mucosa, the most commonly used suture size is:
mcqs.explain: Larger sizes are 2-0 or 0; smaller sizes have more zeros, such as 4-0, 5-0 and 6-0.

mcqs.q: A monofilament suture is characterised by:
opts: Low friction, minimal tissue reaction and high tensile strength, but poor knot-holding
Better knot-holding but capillary action that wicks fluid
High friction and marked tissue reaction
Absorbability by hydrolysis in all cases
mcqs.explain: Polyfilament (braided) sutures give better strength, handling and knot-holding, but their capillary action can wick fluid and spread bacteria.

saqs.q: Name the scalpel blades used in oral surgery and the main indication of each.
saqs.a: No. 15 — commonest, flaps and incisions around teeth and on edentulous ridges. No. 12 — hooked, gingival sulcus and posterior to teeth. No. 11 — sharp pointed, small stab incisions. No. 10 — larger, extra-oral skin incisions.

head: Blade
Main indication
rows: the commonest — flaps and incisions around teeth and on edentulous ridges
hooked — incisions in the gingival sulcus and posterior to teeth (maxillary tuberosity)
sharp pointed — small stab incisions, e.g. incising an abscess

saqs.q: Describe the No. 9 Molt periosteal elevator and how each end is used.
saqs.a: It has a sharp pointed end and a broader rounded end. The POINTED end starts the periosteal reflection and reflects the dental papillae from between the teeth; the BROAD ROUNDED end continues elevating the periosteum from the bone in a single layer.

head: End
Use
rows: starts the periosteal reflection, and reflects the dental papillae from between the teeth
continues elevating the periosteum from the bone, in a single layer

saqs.q: Why should a surgical (not air-turbine) handpiece be used for bone removal, and what precaution reduces bone necrosis?
saqs.a: A surgical handpiece is high-torque, completely sterilizable, and does not exhaust air into the wound. The air-turbine drill must not be used because air forced into deeper tissue planes causes surgical (air) EMPHYSEMA. To avoid heat-induced bone necrosis, cut with copious saline coolant.

ans.text: A dedicated surgical handpiece is high-torque, completely sterilizable, and does not exhaust air into the wound.
The routine air-turbine drill must not be used — air forced into deeper tissue planes can cause surgical (air) emphysema, a dangerous condition.
To avoid heat-induced bone necrosis, cut with copious saline coolant.

saqs.q: Classify suture materials with examples, and state the common oral suture and size.
saqs.a: ABSORBABLE (hydrolysis) — Monocryl, Vicryl, Chromic, PDS. NON-ABSORBABLE — Nylon (Ethilon), Gortex, Silk, Prolene, Steel. Commonest oral suture is black silk, size 3-0 (000). Monofilament: low friction, high tensile strength, poor knot holding. Polyfilament (braided): better handling and knots, but capillary action can spread bacteria.

ans.text: The commonest non-resorbable suture in the mouth is black silk; the commonest size for oral mucosa is 3-0 (000).

head: MONOFILAMENT
POLYFILAMENT (braided)
rows: low friction, high tensile strength — but poor knot holding
handles and knots better — but shows capillary action that can spread bacteria

saqs.q: List the three main types of dental elevator and the maxillary extraction forceps and their beak features.
saqs.a: ELEVATORS — straight (commonest), triangular/Cryer (broken root with an empty adjacent socket), pick/Apexo (double-angled, root tips). MAXILLARY FORCEPS — anterior (straight handles, concave rounded beaks), premolar/universal (S-shaped, concave), molar (left/right, pointed buccal beak and concave palatal), third-molar bayonet (longest, smooth concave both sides), root bayonet (straight handles, narrow angled concave beaks).

head: Type
Use
rows: a broken root with an empty adjacent socket

head: Forceps
Beak features
rows: left/right specific — a pointed buccal beak (for the buccal bifurcation) and a concave palatal beak
the longest; smooth concave beaks, for both sides
straight handles, narrow angled concave beaks, for all upper roots

saqs.q: Describe the retractors used in oral surgery and the correct way to use a retractor.
saqs.a: Retractors give access and vision, protect soft tissue and expose the field. AUSTIN — right-angle, cheek/tongue/flaps. MINNESOTA — offset, cheek and flap. SELDIN — retracts soft tissue; looks like a periosteal elevator but its edge is NOT sharp, so never use it to elevate mucoperiosteum. WEIDER — broad heart-shaped serrated tongue retractor. CORRECT USE — place the edge ON BONE, so force does not rest on the flap.

ans.text: Good access and vision are essential; retractors also protect soft tissue from cutting instruments and expose the field.

head: Retractor
Description
rows: a right-angle retractor for the cheek, tongue or flaps
an offset retractor for the cheek and flap
retracts oral soft tissue; looks like a periosteal elevator but its leading edge is NOT sharp, so it must not be used to elevate the mucoperiosteum
broad, heart-shaped, serrated — engages the tongue and retracts it medially and anteriorly

ans.text: Correct use — the retractor edge is placed ON BONE to retract the reflected flap, so that the force does not rest on the flap itself.
